text: Every chapter so far has taught you how to attack like a real adversary. This chapter asks a different question: once you can do that, what's the most useful way to use it? Red team, blue team, and purple team all use the same underlying skills, but they're organized around completely different goals, and understanding what actually changes between them is the key to this whole chapter.

A red team engagement simulates a real attacker going after a real objective, chaining recon, access, and lateral movement while trying hard not to get caught. The blue team — the SOC analysts and detection engineers you met earlier in this path — isn't told it's happening. That blindness is deliberate. If defenders know an attack is coming this afternoon, every dashboard gets watched closely, and the test tells you nothing about an ordinary day three months from now.

Purple teaming takes those same two skill sets and removes the fog of war on purpose. Red team measures real-world readiness slowly, through a report delivered weeks later. The blue team's detection function is present in every mode. But only purple teaming puts attacker and defender in direct, real-time dialogue — one technique at a time, with an immediate answer to 'did it fire?' instead of a finding buried in a document.

Inside an actual purple team session, red announces a specific technique, executes it, and tells blue exactly what just happened. Blue checks the SIEM in real time — did an alert fire, and how fast? If it didn't, both sides diagnose the gap together, right there: a missing log source, a detection rule that's too narrow, or a rule that exists but was never actually deployed.

That's the real trade-off. Purple teaming gives up the blind, true-to-life measurement that makes a red team engagement honest. In exchange, it gets every gap it finds fixed in the same session, instead of waiting for the next red team engagement to confirm whether it's still broken. Mature security programs don't choose one over the other — they run red team engagements on a cadence to measure real readiness, and purple team exercises in between to drive detection coverage up fast against the techniques that matter most.

Knowing the difference is step one. Next lesson, you'll walk through the real structure of a purple team session itself — how techniques get chosen, how the exercise is run technique by technique, and how a working session stays productive instead of turning into an unfocused back-and-forth.
